title: The sakhis close
hook: the travels, the tests, the laughter and the lessons

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangat: slow at the turn, the lesson said once. Your line was pass it on. Who did you tell a story to? Did they ask for it again? Day seven hundred forty-six.

Boiling oil gone cool. A dead pipal tree turning green. Bitter soapnuts that tasted sweet. A pot cooking on an eclipse day while the crowd shouted. A boy watching kindling catch. A robber setting down treasure because he'd tasted salt. That's a lot of road for twenty-five days. This block opened the janamsakhis, the life-stories of Guru Nanak, and walked through them one sakhi at a time. Today we stop at the end of the road and look back. The sakhis close.
screen: `OIL GONE COOL. SOAPNUTS MADE SWEET.` → `A ROBBER SETS DOWN THE TREASURE.` → `LOOKING BACK DOWN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the books. We met the families of janamsakhis: the old Puratan telling, the Bala telling, Miharban's thoughtful one, the illustrated pages. We learned how to read a sakhi: not a news report, but truth in the shape of a story. Then the people around Nanak. Mata Sulakhni, who kept the home going. Sri Chand, who chose a different path. Parents in Talwandi asking him to stay. Then the travels and the tests. Kauda and the oil. Mardana bewitched and sung free. Bitter fruit made sweet. The yogis' seat. Cooking at the eclipse. The learned man of Benares. Farid's verses kept at Pakpattan. The king of the island, waiting. Then endings and beginnings. Mardana's last song, and the rabab handed on. A boy by the fire who became Baba Buddha. Two villages, settle here, scatter there. Bhumia's three promises. And last, how the sakhis live: differing in the details while the lesson stays, painted on walls, told aloud to children. Look across all of it and a pattern shows. In these sakhis, the tests aren't won by force. The oil cools, the robber keeps his word, the pandit listens to a song. And there's laughter in it, too: a Guru blessing the rude village to stay home. Tomorrow a new block begins, and the voices change. The Guru Granth Sahib holds the words of the Gurus and also of Bhagats, holy poets from different backgrounds. We met Kabir and Farid already. Next, the Bhagats in their own voices.
screen: `THE BOOKS, AND HOW TO READ THEM.` · `THE PEOPLE AROUND NANAK.` · `TRAVELS, TESTS AND ENDINGS.` · `HOW SAKHIS LIVE ON.` · then, large: `MY FAVORITE SAKHI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your favorite sakhi. Let them pass by in the sit, one at a time, like pictures on a wall. The oil. The soapnuts. Mardana's rabab. The boy and the kindling. The two villages. Bhumia and the salt. Don't think too hard. Notice which one you keep coming back to, the one that tugs. That's yours. Then ask it one question: what do you know that I need today? If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Janamsakhi. A collection of life-stories of Guru Nanak, the sakhis this block walked through one at a time, from the travels and tests to the endings and beginnings.
Your line: my favorite sakhi. Today, tell someone which sakhi you chose and why, in three sentences or fewer. Day seven hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs return to the sakhis of Guru Nanak's life in katha, at gurpurab celebrations and at home, and families have favorites they tell again.
